subject: mathematics
question_text: If A is the matrix with rows (cos α, sin α) and (−sin α, cos α), then show that AAᵀ = AᵀA = I.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), chapter 5 MATRICES, Very Short Answer question 9, book p.33. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1 split gives one mark to each product, because the question asks for two products and a student who computes only AAᵀ has answered half of it. NOTATION: the book prints the transpose as A¹ (a clipped dash); it is written here as Aᵀ, which is the form the rest of this unit uses, and the mathematics is unchanged. CHECKED: both products were expanded position by position and every diagonal entry reduced to cos²α + sin²α = 1 and every off-diagonal entry to cos α sin α − sin α cos α = 0, so both land on I. Related card in the same unit: ts_ipe_m1a_mat_sqp_rotation_inverse asks for the adjoint and inverse of the closely related matrix with rows (cos α, −sin α) and (sin α, cos α); this one asks for the two transpose products, so the two are not duplicates. Paper position: Maths-1A Section A runs Q1 to Q10 at 2 marks each, all compulsory, under the 2026-27 pattern. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would show that this matrix times its transpose is the unit matrix.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Write Aᵀ and form AAᵀ
steps.margin_note: First mark. Aᵀ swaps rows with columns, so the two off-diagonal entries change places. A is 2×2, so both products are 2×2.
steps.memory_tip: Transposing this matrix only moves the minus sign from the lower left to the upper right.

recall.must_convey: That Aᵀ is written by swapping rows and columns, and AAᵀ multiplies out to the unit matrix using cos²α + sin²α = 1.
accept: write A transpose then multiply A by it and use cos squared plus sin squared equals one
the diagonal entries become one and the other two cancel to zero
A times A transpose gives the identity matrix
A transpose rasi multiply cheste diagonal lo one, migilinavi zero
row times column gives cos squared alpha plus sin squared alpha

steps.why: The whole result rests on one identity, cos²α + sin²α = 1, on the diagonal, and on the two products cancelling off the diagonal. Writing the entries out is what shows it.
common_mistakes: Writing Aᵀ with the minus sign left in the lower left corner.
Multiplying entry by entry instead of row by column.

steps.label: Form AᵀA and conclude
steps.margin_note: Second mark. AᵀA has to be computed separately — matrix multiplication is not commutative in general, so AAᵀ = I does not by itself prove AᵀA = I.
steps.memory_tip: Both products give I, so Aᵀ is the inverse of A. A matrix with this property is called orthogonal.

recall.must_convey: That AᵀA is computed as well and also equals I, so both products give the unit matrix.
accept: do the product the other way round and it is also the identity
A transpose times A also gives one on the diagonal and zero elsewhere
both orders give I so A transpose is the inverse of A
reverse order lo multiply chesina kuda identity vasthundi
the second product is the unit matrix too

steps.why: Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so the second product is a separate calculation. Because both equal I, Aᵀ is the inverse of A.
common_mistakes: Writing 'similarly' and stopping, without showing the second product.
Assuming AAᵀ = AᵀA holds for every square matrix.
